name: Jade Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What happens on a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, hold a two-year technical diploma and lead the electricity company's line crew through the valley. I know the feeder splits and the old poles better than anyone at our depot, and I like hearing a street come back to life after a fault. My knees are stiff after wet climbs, and the small lead pay for the responsibility wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works variable care shifts, and our children are grown and paying their own bills. I earn less than many lineworkers despite leading a crew; we have less than a month of expenses saved and only a few similar jobs nearby. Retirement is in sight but not funded yet, and I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot our crew still has to climb, test and repair the valley power line. A quicker office form might be nice, but I want my apprentices paid for learning the job properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technology picture is mild, but home is already tight. I'm a crew lead on low pay, my partner's care shifts vary and we have less than one month of expenses saved, so one missed wage would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the valley repair roster and check the rigging before each climb. From the next pay packet, we'll put the cost of our monthly streaming bundle into a separate emergency account after cancelling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even with no big AI change. A broken van would be enough to put our retirement plan back another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What ordinary setback makes your savings feel thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A broken crew winch cost two days of work; a broken family van could cost our last month of savings. My pay covered the household bills, but I could not have paid that hire myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew before a climb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the crew to test the rope and winch before anyone climbs. I cannot make their wages stretch further, but I can make sure nobody is rushed onto a bad line.

say: **Valley linework** still needs paid apprentices and physical checks even when office forms shorten.
**Rigging tests** come before any climb, whatever a screen suggests.
think: My **low lead pay** and variable care shifts leave us exposed already.
Less than **one month saved** makes an ordinary household setback serious.
do: **Keep** the valley repair rota and pre-climb rigging checks.
**Cancel** the streaming bundle and cut its monthly charge.
**Save** that bundle cost from each new pay packet for emergencies.
feel: **Anxious** about routine bills despite little technology change.
S0.quote: A broken crew winch cost two days of work; a broken family van could cost our last month of savings.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** follows low pay and less than one month saved, not AI exposure.
She is a **skilled lead** but cannot absorb a small household setback.

steps.text: Keep valley repair rota and pre-climb rigging checks
Cancel streaming bundle and cut its monthly charge
Save streaming cost from each new pay packet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying and booking can move to software, but a program must not decide a crew can skip a wet-ground check. If the company saves office wages, it should pay field crews for the extra checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical line repairs should continue, yet fewer callouts or shorter standby hours would hit us quickly. We have no spare month to wait for the company to notice the loss, and few line jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll record six weeks of paid callouts before and after any new scheduler and bring the comparison to the union branch. At work I'll keep a written list of wrong access notes and ask for a paid stop-work rule when field conditions differ from the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household income and who gets blamed for a bad route. The thinner our reserve, the more a small hours cut matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at a washed-out crossing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the truck at the washed-out crossing and call dispatch for another road. A green route on a tablet will not carry my power-line truck across a washed-out crossing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union branch get from your hours log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the pay slips and the six-week callout log to a branch meeting, then ask members to raise paid checking time with management. I want the rule in writing, not only a verbal assurance.

say: **AI schedules** must leave room for paid field checks and safe route corrections.
Office savings should not become **unpaid crew work** on wet lines.
think: My **callout hours** could realistically shrink as booking becomes faster.
With **under one month** saved and few local alternatives, even a small cut matters.
do: **Record** six weeks of callout pay before and after any new scheduler.
**Take** pay slips and access errors to a union branch meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours and unsafe routing.
S1.quote: A green route on a tablet will not carry my power-line truck across a washed-out crossing.
fieldNote: Her **wage risk** comes from callout hours, not direct replacement of physical repairs yet.
She uses a **union meeting** for a written paid checking rule.

steps.text: Record six weeks of callout pay around new scheduler
Take pay slips and access errors to union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 reaches dispatch first, but field robots around 2031 could take pole repair shifts. We need a written staffing agreement before that machine shows up at our depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our electricity company to cut a big part of this crew once capable robots can climb, and I could be among those sent home. At about 63 I may still need this wage, and our reserve will not cover a long gap. I can lead the best power-line crew in the valley and still lie awake over next month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask our union branch for an urgent meeting on the 2028 dispatch and 2031 field plans. My partner and I will stop the planned kitchen paint job, keep that cash for bills, and seek exact retirement-income figures before discussing any work exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I can picture a large wage loss and I do not know how we'd bridge it. I still have a plan to ask for terms, but the clock feels too short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children what the company has actually said, not put a frightening date on the family calendar. They have their own bills, and I won't ask them to pay ours unless a real emergency arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the branch to negotiate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid transfer places at nearby utilities, though there are only a few, and a clear notice period. I would not pay for a robot course from our last household cash without a funded job attached.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before field robots around 2031 threaten line shifts.
The company should agree **crew numbers and transfers** before field robots arrive.
think: I expect a **large crew cut** and could lose much of my own wage near 63.
Less than **one month saved** leaves almost no bridge to an affordable retirement.
do: **Ask** union branch for urgent meeting on dispatch and field staffing.
**Cancel** planned kitchen paint job and cut that discretionary expense.
**Request** exact retirement-income figures before setting any exit date.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless worry about bills.
S2.quote: I can lead the best power-line crew in the valley and still lie awake over next month's bills.
fieldNote: Her expected **major income loss** and sleeplessness support alarmed rather than merely anxious.
She holds existing paint cash for bills, so **no save-more tag** applies.
Her union request seeks **paid transfers and notice**, not a course enquiry labelled retraining.

steps.text: Ask union branch for urgent dispatch and field staffing meeting
Cancel planned kitchen paint job and cut that expense
Request retirement-income figures before deciding work exit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes planning before field robots reach poles around 2034. Five years lets workers ask for a proper transition agreement instead of a rushed goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 66 I hope I could stop climbing, but our savings are too thin to count on leaving then. The longer warning might help us build a cushion, yet I could still lose shifts before retirement is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union to put paid older-worker inspection posts and apprentice hours on the bargaining agenda. From next pay, we'll send the cancelled streaming charge into savings each month, and I'll keep leading the repair rota while the crew exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage gap, with more time to build a little protection. I need a paid job in the plan, not a kind speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer for a full roster and wage on a ground-inspection post, then compare it with my current pay. A one-day inspection title would not replace the power-line wage that pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would fund the extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The streaming charge is small, but the deposit is new money from each pay packet. If my partner's care shifts fall, we'd use it for bills instead of calling it a retirement fund.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before field robots reach poles around 2034.
Workers need **paid inspection posts** and apprentice hours in any transition agreement.
think: At about **66**, I may still need wages because our savings are thin.
Five years helps, but **crew shifts** could still shrink before retirement works.
do: **Put** paid inspection posts and apprentice hours on the union bargaining agenda.
**Save** streaming charge from new pay while care shifts cover bills.
**Keep** leading valley repairs while the crew has paid work.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic wage gap, with a longer time to prepare.
S3.quote: A one-day inspection title would not replace the power-line wage that pays our bills.
fieldNote: She seeks **full paid posts**, not ceremonial teaching or a course brochure.
The proposed saving is **new pay**, conditional on her partner's care shifts holding.

steps.text: Put paid inspection posts on union bargaining agenda
Save streaming charge from new pay while care shifts cover bills
Keep leading valley repairs while paid crew work remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 changes dispatch before field robots around 2039, when I will be about 71. A decade lets the company plan with workers, but it does not excuse cutting paid training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope I am off regular climbs by 71, though our present savings do not let me promise it. Low pay and variable care shifts still make the next few years anxious even if the robots are far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the line safety tickets current and take our retirement statements to a financial review this year. At the union branch I'll ask for a paid succession plan so younger lineworkers learn the valley network before older crews leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current income, calmer about the far robot date. A long warning gives us room to make demands, not money to pay this month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a younger worker learn on your route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a younger worker where the feeder splits behind the old pump house, then make them test it themselves. A bright arrow on a feeder map cannot replace an apprentice testing a real power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid succession plan contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The succession plan needs paid field days for apprentices and a named worker to hand over each route. I'd bring that proposal to a branch meeting and ask members to put it to management.

say: **2036 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before field robots arrive around 2039.
**Paid apprenticeships** should carry valley knowledge forward before older crews leave.
think: At about **71**, I hope to be off regular climbs, but money does not guarantee it.
Our **thin savings** and care shifts keep the household anxious now.
do: **Renew** line safety tickets while continuing paid repair work.
**Review** actual retirement statements with a financial adviser this year.
**Bring** a paid apprentice succession proposal to the union branch.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, despite a distant robot date.
S4.quote: A bright arrow on a feeder map cannot replace an apprentice testing a real power line.
fieldNote: The far robot date does not erase **baseline income strain** or uncertain retirement.
Her union proposal asks for **paid field days** and named handovers, not vague support.

steps.text: Renew line safety tickets and continue paid repair work
Review retirement statements with financial adviser this year
Bring paid apprentice succession proposal to union branch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable field robots could cut our crew around 2031, when I will be about 63 and still need wages. A written staffing agreement with paid transfer places and enough notice would help us survive a change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the electricity company pays the person who knows every old feeder and trains the next worker. My skill has a name at the power depot, but the household savings account is almost empty. A title will not fill it.

headlineQuote: My skill has a name at the power depot, but the household savings account is almost empty.
portrait: **Jade**, 58, leads difficult valley line repairs with a two-year technical diploma and deep knowledge of old feeders.
Her **low pay**, variable care income, less than one month saved and few local jobs outweigh her high standing.
She has **never used AI** and presses her union for paid safety checks, inspection posts and apprentice field hours.
Fast field robots leave her **alarmed** about a major wage loss; the long scenario still leaves current money anxiety.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring major field crew cuts around 2031 while she still needs line wages.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing agreement** with paid transfer places and enough notice would help the household bridge a change.
